title: America Just Named Indian Food Its Cuisine of the Year — and It Goes Way Beyond Butter Chicken
excerpt: The af&co. + Carbonate 2026 Hospitality Trends Report crowns 'Next-Gen Indian' as the defining food movement, driven by regional cooking, Gen Z spice-seekers, and a doubling of the Indian-American population.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Indian food in America has evolved beyond traditional dishes like butter chicken.
  • The Indian-American population has more than doubled in the last 20 years.
  • Next-Gen Indian cuisine emphasizes regional diversity and authenticity.
  • The ethnic food market in the U.S. is projected to reach $140 billion by 2030.
  • Fast-casual Indian concepts are gaining traction, with significant growth expected.

For decades, Indian food in America lived inside a narrow box: butter chicken, tikka masala, garlic naan, and a lunch buffet that never quite changed. That era is over. The prestigious af&co. + Carbonate 2026 Hospitality Trends Report has officially declared "Next-Gen Indian" the **Cuisine of the Year** — a landmark designation that signals Indian food has graduated from an ethnic niche to the defining force in American dining's next chapter. "Indian cuisine in the U.S. has undergone a remarkable transformation," said Leith Steel, head of insights at creative agency Carbonate. "Over the past two decades — during which the Indian-American population has more than doubled — Indian restaurants have multiplied and diversified, expanding the country's understanding of the cuisine." ## From One India to Many The shift isn't just about more restaurants. It's about *which* restaurants. Where Americans once encountered a generic "Indian" menu heavy on North Indian staples, they're now discovering the vast regional mosaic that Indians have always known: the coconut-laced fish curries of Kerala, the fiery Andhra biryanis, the fermented rice crepes of Tamil Nadu, and the street-food genius of Mumbai's chaat stalls. Datassential, the food industry's leading data firm, has specifically called out **Keralan cuisine** as a breakout trend, noting that Keralan cafes and restaurants are "popping up stateside" with menus built around appam, puttu, and the layered spice work of the Malabar coast. > **"Traditional
$85 billion
Current Value of U.S."** "No longer diluted for American palates, chefs are celebrating the depth of regional Indian cooking," the Carbonate report noted. "From bustling street food and chai cafes to refined tasting menus, Indian wine bars, and cocktail concepts, today's offerings reflect the full vibrancy and sophistication of Indian culture." ## The Grocery Aisle Is Listening The movement extends far beyond restaurant walls. Consumer packaged goods companies are racing to tap the trend: - **Lay's** launched Tikka Masala Kettle Chips - **Miss Vickie's** introduced Tandoori BBQ chips - **Bollygood** rolled out sparkling lemonades infused with pomegranate cardamom, mango turmeric, basil cumin, and ginger mint - **Truly Indian**, a brand of ADF Foods, earned two 2026 NEXTY Awards finalist spots at Natural Products Expo West for its Tikka Masala Naan and Crispy Chili Mango Chutney The broader ethnic food market in the U.S. is now valued at $85 billion, with projections to hit $140 billion by 2030. The "reinvented" ethnic segment — exactly where Next-Gen Indian lives — is growing at twice the rate of traditional ethnic restaurants. ## Why Now? A Perfect Storm Several forces converged to make this moment possible. The Indian-American population has more than doubled in 20 years, creating both a massive consumer base and a deep talent pool of chefs, entrepreneurs, and food storytellers. Meanwhile, Gen Z's well-documented obsession with bold, spicy flavours has made younger diners eager for exactly the kind of maximalist, unapologetic cooking that Indian cuisine delivers. Supply chains have also matured. Specialty ingredients like curry leaves, fresh paneer, and regional spice blends that were once impossible to source outside major metros are now available through expanded distribution networks.
Culinary Innovations in Indian Cuisine
›Keralan cuisine gaining popularity with unique dishes.
›New products like Tikka Masala Kettle Chips launched.
›Fast-casual Indian chains expanding rapidly.
›Gen Z driving demand for bold flavors.
According to Technomic, 52% of American consumers have tried Indian food and liked it. And fast-casual Indian concepts — once dismissed as a pipe dream — are finally gaining real traction, with chains like Tarka Indian Kitchen, Curry Up Now, and Rasa expanding rapidly. ## The Diaspora Angle For the millions of Indian Americans who grew up watching their parents' cooking dismissed as "smelly" or "too spicy," this recognition carries weight that goes beyond industry accolades. It's a cultural validation decades in the making. The designation also creates tangible economic opportunity. Indian-American restaurateurs, food entrepreneurs, and CPG founders now operate in a market that actively wants what they're selling — not a watered-down version of it, but the real thing. "We wanted to change the perception of Indian food as overly spicy and strange, and make it more accessible and healthier," said Sahil Rahman, co-founder of Rasa, the fast-casual concept expanding along the East Coast with backing from investors including a former Starbucks COO. ## What's Next
Cultural Shift in Perception
›Recognition of Indian cuisine as culturally significant.
›Economic opportunities for Indian-American entrepreneurs.
›Changing perceptions of Indian food's complexity.
Industry forecasters predict Indian fast-casual could become a $1 billion segment within the next decade. But the bigger story isn't about any single format — it's about an entire cuisine finally being seen in its full complexity and brilliance. Next-Gen Indian isn't a trend. It's a correction — one that's been 50 years in the making.
